content: C-C chemokine receptor type 1 (CCR1) is a protein encoded by the CCR1 gene in humans. It has also been designated as CD191, which stands for cluster of differentiation 191. This gene encodes a receptor that is part of the beta chemokine receptor family, a subset of G protein-coupled receptors. The receptor binds to specific ligands, including CCL3 (also known as MIP-1 alpha), CCL5 (also referred to as RANTES), CCL7 (or MCP-3), and CCL23 (also called MPIF-1). Chemokines and their receptors play a pivotal role in mediating signal transduction, which is essential for directing effector immune cells to sites of inflammation. Studies involving knockout models of the mouse homolog of CCR1 have demonstrated its importance in host defense mechanisms. These studies suggest that CCR1 is involved in protecting the host from inflammatory responses and influences susceptibility to viral and parasitic infections. Additionally, the CCR1 gene is located within a gene cluster on chromosome 3p, along with other chemokine receptor genes such as CCR2, CCRL2, CCR3, CCR5, and CXCR1. CCR1 has been shown to interact specifically with the chemokine ligand CCL5.
